questions.q: A refracting telescope in normal adjustment has an objective lens of focal length 0.90 m and an eyepiece of focal length 0.030 m. What is its angular magnification?
questions.solution: In normal adjustment the angular magnification is the focal length of the objective divided by that of the eyepiece: \(M = \frac{f_{o}}{f_{e}} = \frac{0.90}{0.030}\) = 30. The lenses are 0.93 m apart, which is the sum of the focal lengths, not the magnification.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of a reflecting telescope over a refracting telescope?

options.A: Its mirror does not cause chromatic aberration.
options.B: It does not need an eyepiece or detector.
options.C: It can only observe radio waves.
options.D: Its image is never affected by the atmosphere.

questions.solution: A mirror reflects all wavelengths in the same way, so it gives no chromatic aberration; a lens refracts different colours by different amounts. Large mirrors can also be supported from behind, so they can be made much bigger than lenses.

questions.q: A telescope with an aperture of diameter 2.0 m observes light of wavelength \(5.0 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}\). Using the Rayleigh criterion, what is the smallest angular separation it can resolve?
questions.solution: \(\theta \approx \frac{\lambda}{D} = \frac{5.0 \times 10^{-7}}{2.0} = 2.5 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{rad}\). A larger aperture resolves finer detail.

questions.q: The diameter of a telescope's objective is doubled. What happens to its collecting power?

options.C: It increases by a factor of four.
options.D: It increases by a factor of eight.

questions.solution: Collecting power is proportional to the area of the objective, and so to its diameter squared. Doubling the diameter collects four times as much light each second, so fainter objects can be seen.

questions.q: Star X has an apparent magnitude of one and star Y has an apparent magnitude of six. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Y appears a hundred times brighter than X.
options.B: X appears a hundred times brighter than Y.
options.C: X appears five times brighter than Y.
options.D: Y appears five times brighter than X.

questions.solution: A smaller magnitude means a brighter star. Each step of one magnitude is a factor of about 2.51 in brightness, and a difference of five magnitudes is a factor of exactly one hundred.

questions.q: A star has an apparent magnitude of 7.0 and is 100 pc away. What is its absolute magnitude?
questions.solution: \(m - M = 5\log\left(\frac{d}{10}\right)\), with \(d\) in parsecs. Here \(\log\left(\frac{100}{10}\right)\) is one, so the difference is five magnitudes: M = 7.0 − 5 = 2.0. The star would look brighter from the standard distance of 10 pc.

questions.q: A star has a surface temperature of 5800 K. At what wavelength is its black-body radiation most intense? (Wien's constant \(2.9 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m K}\))
questions.solution: Wien's displacement law: \(\lambda_{max}T = 2.9 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m K}\). So \(\lambda_{max} = \frac{2.9 \times 10^{-3}}{5800} = 5.0 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}\), in the visible range.

questions.q: Two stars have the same radius. Star X has twice the surface temperature (in kelvin) of star Y. How does the power output of X compare with that of Y?

options.B: It is four times as large.
options.C: It is eight times as large.
options.D: It is sixteen times as large.

questions.solution: Stefan's law: \(P = \sigma AT^{4}\). With the same surface area, the power is proportional to the temperature to the fourth power. Twice the temperature gives two to the fourth power: sixteen times the power.

questions.q: Which spectral class contains the hottest stars?
questions.solution: The spectral classes in order of falling temperature are O, B, A, F, G, K, M. Class O stars are the hottest and look blue; class M stars are the coolest and look red. The Sun is class G.

questions.q: On a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, with temperature decreasing to the right, where are white dwarfs found?
questions.solution: White dwarfs are hot but very small, so they are dim: hot puts them on the left, dim puts them at the bottom. Red giants and supergiants are cool but very bright, at the top right. The main sequence runs from top left to bottom right.

questions.q: Which sequence describes the future evolution of a star like the Sun?

options.A: Main sequence, supergiant, supernova, neutron star
options.B: Main sequence, red giant, white dwarf
options.C: Main sequence, white dwarf, red giant
options.D: Main sequence, red giant, black hole

questions.solution: When hydrogen in the core runs out, a star of the Sun's mass swells into a red giant. It later sheds its outer layers as a planetary nebula, leaving the hot core as a white dwarf. Only much more massive stars end as supernovae, neutron stars or black holes.

questions.q: What is the Schwarzschild radius of a black hole of mass \(2.0 \times 10^{31}\ \text{kg}\)? (\(G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^{2}\ \text{kg}^{-2}\), \(c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\))
questions.solution: \(R_{s} = \frac{2GM}{c^{2}} = \frac{2 \times 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 2.0 \times 10^{31}}{(3.00 \times 10^{8})^{2}} = 3.0 \times 10^{4}\ \text{m}\). This is the radius of the event horizon, inside which the escape velocity is greater than the speed of light.

questions.q: Why can type 1a supernovae be used as standard candles?

options.A: They are the nearest objects to the Earth.
options.B: They all have the same apparent brightness.
options.C: They are always found in our own galaxy.
options.D: They all reach the same known peak luminosity, so their distance can be found from how bright they appear.

questions.solution: A standard candle is an object of known luminosity. Type 1a supernovae all reach nearly the same peak absolute magnitude. Comparing that with how bright one appears gives its distance, even for very distant galaxies.

questions.q: A spectral line has a wavelength of 500.0 nm in the laboratory. In the light from a galaxy it is observed at 505.0 nm. How fast is the galaxy receding? (\(c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\))
questions.solution: Red shift: \(z = \frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda} = \frac{5.0}{500.0} = 0.010\). For speeds much less than light, \(z = \frac{v}{c}\), so \(v = 0.010 \times 3.00 \times 10^{8} = 3.0 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\).

questions.q: A galaxy is 200 Mpc away. Taking the Hubble constant as \(70\ \text{km s}^{-1}\ \text{Mpc}^{-1}\), what is its recession speed?
questions.solution: Hubble's law: \(v = Hd = 70 \times 200 = 1.4 \times 10^{4}\ \text{km s}^{-1}\). With the distance in megaparsecs and the constant in these units, the speed comes out in \(\text{km s}^{-1}\).

questions.q: How does the transit method detect a planet orbiting another star?

options.A: By seeing the planet directly through a telescope.
options.B: By measuring the red shift of the planet's light.
options.C: By detecting a regular small dip in the star's brightness as the planet passes in front of it.
options.D: By detecting radio signals from the planet.

questions.solution: When a planet crosses the face of its star as seen from Earth, it blocks a little of the star's light. The dip repeats once every orbit. The other main method looks for a wobble in the star's own spectrum, a changing Doppler shift, caused by the planet's pull.
